1. Introduction
Hypothesis testing is one of the oldest and most widely studied problems in statistical inference,
and is critical in research for nearly every scientific branch. Simply put, hypothesis testing asks,
given a collection of N data points X = {X (1) , . . . , X (N ) }, whether the data points come from a
distribution proposed by a null hypothesis H0 or by an alternative hypothesis H1 .
    Classical hypothesis testing often focuses on univariate or discrete distributions. However, these
distributions may be insufficient in many applications. For instance, if we wish to test a hypothesis
on patient data, each patient may have numerous features such as those corresponding to vitals,
organ function, metabolic rate, presence or severity of diseases, etc. Consequently, it is crucial to
develop hypothesis testing procedures for high-dimensional distributions.
    In many practical applications of hypothesis testing, the data may reveal highly sensitive in-
formation about an individual. For instance, the data may include whether a patient has a certain
disease, or has participated in a crime or embarrassing activity. For this reason, an increasingly

does not affect the output of the algorithm significantly. Hence, an adversary cannot reconstruct any
single user’s data based on the algorithm’s output, thereby ensuring that each user’s data is secure.
    In this paper, we study differentially private hypothesis testing for high-dimensional distribu-
tions. We primarily study two major classes of distributions: multivariate Gaussians and Boolean
product distributions. Specifically, we consider the following problems, as well as certain general-

   1. How many samples from a multivariate Gaussian distribution N (µ, Σ), where µ ∈ Rd is the
      mean vector and Σ ∈ Rd×d is the covariance matrix, are necessary to privately determine
      whether µ = µ∗ for some fixed µ∗ ∈ Rd or µ is “far” from µ∗ ?

   2. How many samples from a product distribution D over {−1, 1}d are necessary to privately

1.1. Private Hypothesis Testing
In this subsection, we describe the basics of differential privacy and differentially private hypothesis

1.2. Our Results
In all of the problems we investigate, our goal is to devise an algorithm A that can (ε, δ)-privately
distinguish between a null hypothesis H0 and an alternative hypothesis H1 , where the number of
samples N is as small as possible. We also are interested in constructing such an algorithm that is
efficient, meaning that the runtime is polynomial in the number of samples N and the dimension d.

1.3. Related Work
Ignoring privacy constraints, hypothesis testing from a statistical point of view dates back nearly
a century, notably to Neyman and Pearson (1933). Hypothesis testing has become a popular area
of study in theoretical computer science more recently (where it is also called distribution testing),
starting with (Goldreich and Ron, 2000; Batu et al., 2000), and with a large body of subsequent
literature over the past two decades (see, for instance, (Canonne, 2020) for a survey of the distribu-
tion testing field). While much of the work has focused on discrete or univariate distributions, there
has recently been significant work in the multivariate setting as well. This work on multivariate
hypothesis testing has come both from statistical (Hotelling, 1931; Srivastava and Du, 2008; Chen
and Qin, 2010; Cai and Ma, 2013; Javanmard and Montanari, 2014; Ramdas et al., 2016) and com-
putational (Alon et al., 2007; Rubinfeld and Xie, 2010; Acharya et al., 2015; Daskalakis and Pan,
2017; Acharya et al., 2018a; Daskalakis et al., 2018; Gheissari et al., 2018; Bezáková et al., 2020;
Canonne et al., 2020a; Diakonikolas and Kane, 2021) perspectives.
     Differentially private hypothesis testing began with work by Vu and Slavkovic (2009); Uhler
et al. (2013), and has seen significant work during the past decade. Apart from the work by Canonne
et al. (2020b), which this paper primarily improves over, perhaps the work most closely related to
ours is that of Cai et al. (2017); Aliakbarpour et al. (2018); Acharya et al. (2018b), which study
the problem of private identity testing (as well as closeness testing) of discrete distributions. Var-
ious other problems in private hypothesis testing have also been studied, including testing simple
hypotheses (Cummings et al., 2018; Canonne et al., 2019), selection from a discrete set of mul-
tiple hypotheses (Bun et al., 2019), goodness-of-fit and independence testing (Wang et al., 2015;
Gaboardi et al., 2016; Rogers and Kifer, 2017; Kakizaki et al., 2017; Aliakbarpour et al., 2019),

In this subsection, we note several reductions between problems that will make things easier to

     First, we note the asymptotic equivalence between (ε, δ)-DP and (ε + δ, 0)-DP in the hypothesis
testing case. Roughly, this follows because we assume the probability of acceptance/rejection has

C.1. On changing the construction of Canonne et al. (2020b)
An important part of both our argument and the argument of Canonne et al. (2020b) for the ineffi-
cient testing algorithm was that the statistic F on the subset C is D-Lipschitz. The previous work
of Canonne et al. (2020b) made the subtle mistake of assuming that it suffices for any two adjacent
datasets X , X ′ in C to satisfy |F (X ) − F (X ′ )| ≤ D. In reality, we need that for any datasets
X , X ′ ∈ C that differ in K positions (for any K ≤ N ), |F (X ) − F (X ′ )| ≤ D · K. It is reasonable
to believe these definitions are equivalent: indeed, if X , X ′ ∈ C differ by K positions, then we can
construct a series of adjacent datasets X =: X (0) , X (1) , X (2) , . . . , X (N ) := X ′ where X (i−1) and
X (i) are adjacent. A natural guess is that if X , X ′ ∈ C, then one can ensure that each X (i) is also
in C. If so, then a triangle inequality implies the statistic F is D-Lipschitz on C, as long as adjacent
datasets in C have the statistic differ by at most D.
    Unfortunately, it may be impossible to make the intermediate datasets X (i) be in C for the
choice of C used in Canonne et al. (2020b). Indeed, the choice of C used in Canonne et al. (2020b)
was the set of data X = {X (1) , . . . , X (N ) } (where each X (i) ∈ Rd ) such that ∥X (i) ∥2 ≤ ∆ and
|⟨X (i) , X (1) +· · ·+X (N ) ⟩| ≤ ∆ for some appropriate choice of ∆. However, even if N = 2, d = 3,
and K = 2, we lose our desired property. For instance, define a = (1, 0, 1), b = (−1, 0, 1), c =
(0, 1, 1), and d = (0, −1, 1) to be points in Rd . Let C be the set of pairs {X (1) , X (2) } such that
∥X (i) ∥2 ≤ 2 and |⟨X (i) , X (1) + X (2) ⟩| ≤ 2, for both i = 1 and i = 2. It is clear that the sets
{a, b} and {c, d} are in C, and they differ in K = 2 positions. However, any method of 2 steps
used to convert {a, b} to {c, d} cannot stay in C throughout, because one can see that none of
{a, c}, {a, d}, {b, c}, or {b, d} are in C.
